title: A. Paññāvaddho: The pure citta is Nibbāna. The citta that we experience is the citta that has been usurped by the kilesas. And because of…
content:
Understanding the Nature of the Pure Citta and Nibbāna

The pure citta is Nibbāna. The citta that we experience is the citta that has been usurped by the kilesas. And because of that usurpation by the kilesas, the citta is constantly changing. In the ultimate sense, we can say that Nibbāna is always there, and that even the functioning of the kilesas is part of the situation. The relationship of the citta to Nibbāna is difficult to describe. The citta is not an object of awareness; it's more like a function of awareness. It is difficult to put into words, because everything we know in this world is impermanent, constantly changing. So we know the citta only in its changingness, in the way it changes all the time. When it comes to the pure citta, it is impossible to know it in the way we know the nature of change, because the pure citta has no duality. When there is no duality, we have no means by which we can know it, except for the knowing nature of the citta itself. That goes rather high.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The Buddha offered several antidotes to the greedy mentality, stating that the path beyond greed begins with generosity. When we give freely of…
content:
Generosity, Contentment, and Moderation as Antidotes

The Buddha offered several antidotes to the greedy mentality, stating that the path beyond greed begins with generosity. When we give freely of our possessions, our time, and our kindness, we actively weaken the grip of "me" and "mine". We experience the joy that comes from benefiting others rather than just ourselves. Core Buddhist values such as contentment with less and a commitment to moderation also act as antidotes. Contentment allows us to appreciate what we have instead of obsessing over what we lack. Moderation breaks the cycle of greed by helping us recognize when we have enough—that point of sufficiency where mind and body are properly maintained without excess. Both contentment and moderation help loosen the grip of self-centeredness.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "To overcome evil, we need the power and quickness of a true moral reflex to help us fight against the cunning and deceit…
content:
The Power of a Moral Reflex

"To overcome evil, we need the power and quickness of a true moral reflex to help us fight against the cunning and deceit of our mental defilements. Hiri and ottappa can sense when we are about to do, say, or even think something harmful—sometimes even before our mindfulness becomes aware of the danger. Thus, they are an effective early warning system. The unerring information they provide us about right and wrong is necessary for speaking and acting without causing harm. Abandoning evil is virtually impossible without them. By cultivating hiri and ottappa within ourselves, we not only accelerate our own progress along the path to freedom from suffering but also do our part to safeguard the world and the people around us. The Buddha called these two qualities the guardians of the world, and with good reason."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "There is the mundane way of communication, which is ordinary speech; and there’s a higher way of communication, which, although more accurate, is…
content:
The Pitfalls of Higher Communication

"There is the mundane way of communication, which is ordinary speech; and there’s a higher way of communication, which, although more accurate, is also elusive and formless. Trying to communicate direct understanding in the higher way, using metaphorical terms, can be more confusing than using the ordinary way of speech. In ordinary speech, we use logic, reason, experience and memory. Although the explanations are a bit makeshift, they can gradually lead to understanding. But when the ordinary person tries to explain Dhamma in high-sounding metaphors, the explanation usually turns out quite messy because there’s so much scope for the kilesas to intrude and distort one’s thinking."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The skin is a great deceiver because it covers up all the other parts and makes them look presentable. What if we were…
content:
The Deception of the External Layer

The skin is a great deceiver because it covers up all the other parts and makes them look presentable. What if we were to take this skin off and look underneath – we would get a completely different picture. But we see only the outside layer and deduce that the body is beautiful and desirable. At the same time skin is an essential factor in how this body functions – without it we would die. All of this we may know perfectly well in theory, but we fail to see the implications of skin as far as our sense of self is concerned. In fact skin is just something which belongs to this world – it comes from the world and it goes back to the world. Skin is not “me”. It has nothing to do with who I truly am, so how can it be me?

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "There is also an ultimate reality, but we can't use words to describe it. By its very nature it’s beyond language. Because words…
content:
The Nature of Conventional Truth

"There is also an ultimate reality, but we can't use words to describe it. By its very nature it’s beyond language. Because words are relative things, whatever we might say about it is relative. Words are only symbols. We can talk about bottles and concrete and other material things because we can refer directly to those objects. There is always a relationship between us and them. But with paramattha, or ultimate truth, there is nothing you can point to. In a court of law one must tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. There we are dealing with conventional truth. The basis of conventional truth is mutual acceptance. When people agree on certain conventions they become accepted truth. This principle applies to sense data as well. The way we define the things we see and the distinctions we make between visual objects are matters of convention. It’s practical of course. The conventional view of the world that we have been taught since childhood has become such a deeply-ingrained part of us that it seems quite natural."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Theory can only take us so far; real understanding comes from investigating our own experience, especially those experiences that occur within the field…
content:
Timeless Dhamma Truth vs. Shifting Scientific Models

"Theory can only take us so far; real understanding comes from investigating our own experience, especially those experiences that occur within the field of our conscious awareness. Only then can we see the true relationship between mind and reality, between the knower and the known. When we look deeply into the basis of scientific knowledge, we see that it rests upon shifting sands. Each new discovery overwrites what came before, so what scientists hold as absolute truth today may later be discarded as ineffective. How different this is from what the Lord Buddha realized... those truths that are timeless, unchanging, and point directly to the heart of our human predicament. What science offers us are conventional truths, which may be useful for worldly purposes but cannot touch the deeper truths that the Buddha discovered. Those conventional truths are like the reflection of the moon in water: constantly shifting, breaking apart, and reforming. While "Dhamma" truth is like the moon itself: unchanging and reliable in its orbit.",

title: A. Paññāvaddho: The core problem with an untamed mind lies in its perpetual restlessness. Like a monkey jumping from branch to branch, it cannot remain…
content:
Samadhi as the Remedy for the Mind’s Habitual Restlessness

The core problem with an untamed mind lies in its perpetual restlessness. Like a monkey jumping from branch to branch, it cannot remain still even when physically at rest. When the mind lacks the protection of Dhamma, it mistakes momentary sensual gratification for true happiness. But these fleeting pleasures only reinforce its unruly nature. Much like giving sweets to a child throwing a tantrum, it may bring temporary quiet, but ultimately it strengthens the bad behavior. This is why samadhi is so crucial. It stands as a direct antidote to the mind's habitual resistance to discipline. The stability of mind achieved through samadhi is like driving a stake deep into the ground. It provides an anchor point from which all other mental development can proceed. Yet the mind, so long accustomed to its wandering ways, stubbornly rebels against the lifeline that meditation objects offer. This resistance isn't unusual; it's the accumulated result of countless lifetimes of indulging in sensual pleasures and following defilements. Those who truly understand this predicament—this endless wandering through samsara due to an untamed mind—must develop an unwavering commitment to their meditation practice.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Actually, samādhi is not really an intellectual training at all. It’s an emotional one. The reason why samādhi is so valuable is that…
content:
Samādhi as Emotional Training for Wisdom Investigation

"Actually, samādhi is not really an intellectual training at all. It’s an emotional one. The reason why samādhi is so valuable is that it corrects the emotions and it makes them strong in the right way. And when they’re strong in a right way, if you see anything that is really quite horrific when you are investigating with wisdom, you can withstand it easily because strong samādhi brings a state of great calm. When a state of great calm is present, the mind is happy and content, so the kilesas have no reason to come up and cause trouble. As long as the kilesas don't come up, the mind is free to turn and do some meaningful investigation. And it can do so without fear of harmful effects. But you must be careful when investigating without the proper development of samādhi to stabilize the mind. For instance, when contemplating the significance of anicca, if you see the truth of anicca very profoundly, the experience can be quite devastating."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The nature of existence can be expressed as a paradox. We can say that anything that changes is not real, because it does…
content:
The Paradox of Existence Versus the Reality of Nibbāna

"The nature of existence can be expressed as a paradox. We can say that anything that changes is not real, because it does not last. So what exists is not real and what is real does not exist. Thus reality and existence are two opposites. The world of our sensual experiences is an aspect of existence because nothing remains the same from one moment to the next. Nothing we experience is fixed and immutable; all is flowing and changing. Nibbāna is the one that is not changing. And Nibbāna is there within each one of us. It’s our true nature. Really speaking, we should all be in the state of Nibbāna. Arahants are the only people who are normal. Because we have kilesas, all the rest of us are a bit peculiar. When we get rid of the kilesas, there is nothing to disturb the citta. When the citta is completely undisturbed, it automatically goes to Nibbāna."
